newsitem.title: UK: Global warming means more Australian wheat - study.
newsitem.headline: Global warming means more Australian wheat - study.

text.p: Global warming has helped Australian farmers reap bumper crops of wheat, researchers reported on Wednesday.
They said careful analysis had shown the steady increase in temperatures had created a number of effects that translated into bigger harvests.

"Climate trends appear to be responsible for 30 to 50 percent of the observed increase in wheat yields, with increases in minimum temperature being the dominant influence," Neville Nicholls of the Bureau of Meteorology Research Centre in Melbourne wrote in a letter to the science journal Nature.
"The average yield of wheat, Australia's major crop, has increased by about half a tonne per hectare since 1952," he added.
There were several effects climate could have on a crop, Nicholls said. One was frequency of frosts.

"The frequency of severe frosts has decreased in eastern Australia in recent decades," he wrote. "Changes in rainfall and soil moisture would also affect yield, while an increase in mean daily temperature would decrease yield."

His team had measured these factors. "Mean annual maximum temperatures, averaged across Australia, increased by 0.58 degree C from 1952 to 1992. Mean annual minimum temperatures increased by 1.02 degrees C (1.8 degree F), while mean annual rainfall only increased by 39 mm," he wrote.
Nicholls said his team had factored in for changes in pesticide and fertiliser use and improvements in agricultural methods. Even with these considered, the yields had improved.

Nearly all climate experts agree that average temperatures are rising around the world. Most also agree that human factors, such as the release of "greenhouse gases" like carbon dioxide, are responsible.
Although Australian wheat farmers are benefiting, global warming is blamed for weather patterns that are helping the Sahara desert grow and causing strong cyclones in tropical areas.
